item.title: Fighting for Growth: Labor Scarcity and Technological Progress During the British Industrial Revolution
item.headline: When workers became scarce, farms turned to machinery
item.authors: Hans-Joachim Voth, Bruno Caprettini, Alex Trew
item.summary: Wartime recruitment was linked to greater adoption of labor-saving farm machinery in England and Wales. Historical records and assumptions about coastal geography limit the causal interpretation.

evidence.question: Can worker shortages accelerate technology adoption?
evidence.method: Combined recruitment records with machinery listed in 1790–1820 farm-sale advertisements; used deep-water access to predict naval recruitment across 887 coastal areas.
evidence.limitations: Advertisements measure resale, not purchase dates; recruit origins are incompletely recorded.

explainer.finding: Naval recruitment predicted more labor-saving machinery; comparable evidence was absent for other machinery.
explainer.method: Compared coastal areas while accounting for coastline distance, commercial ports, farming conditions and other differences.
explainer.meaning: A thresher replaces hand labor: scarce workers can make buying one more attractive. Adoption matters alongside invention.
explainer.limits: The causal argument assumes deep-water access affects adoption through recruitment. This is not evidence that war improves overall welfare.
